tldr: We developed a pipeline that automatically constructs over 10,000 physics simulation environments from real-world videos, enabling large-scale post-training and fair zero-shot evaluation for coding robot agents. While highlighting the substantial gap between frontier and open-source models in grasping and post-contact control, post-training on high-quality data dramatically lifts an open-source model to a level that works on a physical robot.
hero_caption: Overview of RoboUniverse-10K. (a) An automated Real2Sim pipeline that generates task specifications, physics scenes, and verification code with quality assurance from real-world videos; (b) An unprecedented scale of 10,807 environments compared to existing benchmarks; (c) Performance improvements of an open-source model via SFT (success rate rising from 0.8% to 21.2%) and zero-shot deployment on a physical Franka arm.
overview:
Recently, "Agentic Robotics"—where foundation models (LLMs) act as coding agents to control robots through executable Python scripts and execute perception, planning, and low-level control in a closed loop—has developed rapidly. In software engineering, building massive executable test environments from GitHub pull requests and running post-training (such as SFT and reinforcement learning) dramatically boosted models' coding capabilities. In robotics, however, building simulation environments has relied on manual labor, keeping benchmarks capped at merely a few hundred tasks and causing "Train-on-Test" overfitting to become common practice.

To address this, the authors developed an automated Real2Sim pipeline that generates interactive Isaac Sim environments from real-world robot manipulation videos, creating "RoboUniverse-10K" with 10,807 diverse physics environments. Each environment is packaged in an isolated, secure sandbox (Harbor-compatible) that hides privileged states and ground-truth grading logic, forcing the robot to solve tasks using only real-world-like sensor observations. Furthermore, the authors held out 500 completely unseen tasks verified by experts to establish the "RoboUniverse-Verified" zero-shot benchmark, rigorously evaluating 11 leading proprietary and open-source models.

The results revealed an overwhelming performance gap between frontier models (85.8% for GPT-6.2 Astra) and open-source models (2.6% to 10.0%). Open-source models particularly stumble at the initial "grasping" phase, and even frontier models frequently fail at fine post-contact force control and deformable object manipulation such as cloth. Finally, supervised fine-tuning on an open-source model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) using collected high-quality multi-turn trajectories substantially boosted the success rate from 0.8% to 21.2%, with confirmed zero-shot transfer to unseen external benchmarks and a physical Franka arm.
contributions: Built an automated Real2Sim pipeline that generates and audits physics scenes, reference solutions, and verification logic from real-world manipulation videos, open-sourcing the large-scale collection of 10,807 environments, "RoboUniverse-10K".
Established an execution foundation resilient enough for large-scale reinforcement learning by using Harbor-compatible sandboxes that hide privileged state to mirror real-world sensing constraints.

Established "RoboUniverse-Verified," an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark of 500 tasks, and identified through the evaluation of 11 models that grasping, deformable objects, and post-contact control are current physical bottlenecks.

Post-trained (SFT) an open-source model on 17K multi-turn trajectories (around 0.79B tokens), lifting the success rate from 0.8% to 21.2% and demonstrating zero-shot generalization to other benchmarks and a physical robot.

sections.heading: Toward a Robot SWE-bench: New Horizons Opened by Environment Scaling
sections.summary: While Agentic Robotics—where foundation models write code to control robots—is promising, the high cost of building simulation environments has trapped it in evaluating on the same distribution as training. Following the trajectory of software engineering, this work opens the door to large-scale post-training and rigorous generalization evaluation by automatically generating over 10,000 executable and verifiable simulation environments from real-world videos.
sections.details:
In robot control, Agentic Robotics, where frontier models write Python code to call various APIs, is gaining significant attention compared to traditional end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. The primary driving force behind the dramatic leap in software engineering (SWE) was the ability to run reinforcement learning (RLVR) and distillation on hundreds of thousands of executable environments created from GitHub pull requests (such as SWE-bench). In robotics, however, constructing physically sound scenes and ground-truth success verifiers is difficult, leaving existing benchmarks like LIBERO and RoboCasa capped at just a few hundred tasks.

When environments are small, researchers are forced to evaluate on the exact tasks used during training (Train-on-Test), making it impossible to measure true generalization to unseen scenes. To break through this dual bottleneck—the limit of scale and the lack of generalization benchmarks—the authors proposed an automated pipeline to construct and quality-assure Isaac Sim environments from real-world manipulation videos.

The resulting 10,807 environments (4,132 single-arm Franka and 6,675 dual-arm AgileX) are housed in sandboxes isolated from privileged information. Evaluating 11 models on "RoboUniverse-Verified," an expert-vetted benchmark of 500 completely unseen tasks drawn from the pipeline, revealed that the performance gap between models stems not from high-level task understanding, but from low-level physical control (grasping and fine post-contact manipulation). Furthermore, post-training an open-source model on data collected in these environments enabled zero-shot transfer to diverse settings, including a physical robot.

sections.heading: How to Build 10,000 Tasks? The Automated Real2Sim & QA Pipeline
sections.summary: We built an end-to-end automated pipeline covering video collection, deduplication, object perception and 3D depth estimation, physical property setup, and autonomous quality assurance (QA). Every environment is isolated in a Harbor-compliant sandbox hiding privileged state, running agents under strict, real-world-like observation constraints.
sections.details:
### Agent Harness and Sandbox
Each task is isolated inside a Harbor-compatible sandbox interfaced with an Isaac Sim backend. The agent receives only a natural language instruction and API documentation, executing a Python script to operate the robot. The provided toolset is strictly limited to five functions: `observe()` (retrieves joint states and RGB images), `step()` / `step_chunk()` (sends joint targets and advances physics steps), `finish()` (declares completion), and basic utilities. Privileged object poses and grading criteria are completely hidden, requiring the agent to infer task completion solely from sensor inputs.

### Data Sources and Hierarchical Task Normalization
Videos were sourced from large-scale teleoperation datasets including DROID, BridgeData V2, RT-1, and RoboDojo. Rather than duplicating videos directly, the pipeline defines a 5-level hierarchy: Robot Configuration $\rightarrow$ Task Family $\rightarrow$ Concrete Task $\rightarrow$ Layout $\rightarrow$ Trajectory. Deduplication is performed at the "Concrete Task" level, where interaction types and target objects are fundamentally distinct. As a result, the tasks are organized into 8 major categories across single-arm (Pick & Place, Assembly & Articulation, Deformable & Material, Composite) and dual-arm (Co-Transport, Co-Assembly, Co-Deformable, Staged Coordination), totaling 10,807 tasks.

### Automated Generation and QA Loop
A coding agent builds the environments autonomously. It first extracts task specifications from videos and uses SAM 3.1 (segmentation) and DA3 (depth estimation) to estimate object contours and spatial layouts. Meshes and textures are populated from asset libraries, and physical parameters such as mass, inertia, friction, and joint limits are configured in Isaac Sim. Furthermore, an independent "QA Agent" rigorously audits the generated environment: (1) Fidelity checking semantic and physical alignment with the source video; (2) Reset & Replay checking reproducible execution of reference solutions after resets; and (3) Verifier Audit checking against cheats like clipping or transient goal triggers. If an environment fails, revision directives are issued in an iterative loop until it passes.

captions.F4: The Real2Sim data construction and Quality Assurance (QA) pipeline. Starting from video filtering and task specification, coding agents generate scenes, control code, and verifier code using SAM 3.1 and DA3, followed by audits of fidelity, replayability, and cheat-resistance by an independent QA agent before being packaged into Harbor sandboxes.

sections.heading: The Chasm Between Frontier and Open Models: Bottlenecks in Grasping and Post-Contact
sections.summary: Benchmarking 11 models across 500 expert-vetted zero-shot tasks revealed that while top commercial models reached 85.8%, open-source models peaked at only 10.0%. Physical failure analysis shows that the primary bottleneck is not language understanding, but initial object grasping and fine force control after contact.
sections.details:
### Evaluation Setup and Overall Results
The evaluation utilized 500 tasks (200 single-arm, 300 dual-arm) completely held out from training data. All tasks, reference solutions, and verification logics were validated by 10 human robotics experts. Testing 11 commercial and open-source models exposed a sharp polarization. While top-tier frontier models like GPT-6.2 Astra (85.8%) and Claude Opus 5.5 (76.8%) excelled, the best open-source model was DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 10.0%, with most lingering between 2% and 8%. No model scored between 10% and 49%, representing a massive performance gap.

### Single-Arm vs. Dual-Arm and Task Strengths
Open-source models collapsed especially on dual-arm tasks: while they achieved 6.0% to 18.5% on single-arm, their performance plummeted to 0.3% to 5.3% on dual-arm. Roughly 10% of single-arm tasks are non-prehensile (e.g., knocking over a can or pressing a button), which accounted for about one-third of the lower-tier models' single-arm successes. In contrast, they struggled entirely with dual-arm tasks that almost universally require grasping and 16-DoF coordination.

### Physical Failure Analysis
- **The Grasping Barrier**: While lower-tier models scored 32.1% on non-prehensile tasks, their success collapsed to 0%–4% on tasks requiring grasping. In 46%–47% of failed episodes, failures occurred before touching or lifting the object, with agents executing useless actions until hitting step limits. In other words, they understand the goal, but mapping visual observations to joint angles fails.
- **The Limit on Deformable Objects (Cloth)**: While top models scored high (68%–77%) on rigid-body pick-and-place and assembly, cloth manipulation (like folding towels) remained at a modest 36% even for frontier models. As general model capabilities scaled, cloth manipulation success rose by only 3 points, representing a universal ceiling across all models.
- **Fine Post-Contact Control**: Roughly 80% of frontier model failures occurred *after* establishing contact with objects. Typical failures include sub-centimeter misalignments imperceptible from camera images (e.g., missing a 2mm tolerance by 6mm, leaving a lid unseated) or applying excessive contact forces (70–138N) past a button's 3.5mm stroke limit due to the absence of force feedback.

captions.F5: The decisive performance gap introduced by grasping. (a) In a prehensile task of picking up and uprighting a mug, all frontier models succeed while lower-tier models completely fail. (b) In a non-prehensile task of simply knocking down a can, many lower-tier models succeed, illustrating that low-level grasping is the primary obstacle for open-source models.
captions.F7: Failure modes in fine physical control post-contact. (a) In a lid-capping task, the failed attempt by GPT-6.2 Astra looks visually almost identical to the success by Claude Opus 5.5, but is off-center by 6mm and tilted, failing verification. (b) In a button-pressing task, the lack of force feedback leads to excessive contact force (70–138N) pushed well past the stroke limit.

sections.heading: What Changes with Post-Training? Open Models Acquire Closed-Loop Control
sections.summary: By applying supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B using approximately 17K trajectories collected with GPT-6 Astra, zero-shot success jumped from 0.8% to 21.2%. The model acquired a structured control mindset: forward kinematics modeling, iterative visual adjustments, and state verification, completing zero-shot tasks across external benchmarks and a physical robot.
sections.details:
### Training Setup and Benchmark Results
Using GPT-6 Astra (Medium), the authors collected roughly 17,000 multi-turn manipulation trajectories (totaling 0.79B tokens) across RoboUniverse-10K. Using this as training data, full-parameter SFT was performed on the language backbone of the open-source model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (vision encoder frozen, 256k context length, ~1,500 H100 GPU hours). The resulting "RoboUniverse-35B-A3B" boosted zero-shot success on RoboUniverse-Verified from 0.8% to 21.2%, surpassing all other open-source models and even commercial models like GPT-6 Luna.

### What Did the Model Learn?
A detailed behavioral comparison before and after SFT revealed that the fine-tuned model adopted a systematic three-stage paradigm: "Model $\rightarrow$ Step-and-Check $\rightarrow$ Verify".
1. It computes forward kinematics (FK) and Jacobians from robot parameters to convert Cartesian coordinates into joint angles.
2. It moves in small increments of 3 to 12 cm, adjusting its trajectory in real time based on camera feedback.
3. After releasing an object, it waits for it to come to rest and inspects the image before calling the finish command.

While the base model searched joint space blindly and output lengthy, ungrounded reflections (wasting tokens at a median length 14 times longer than the SFT model), SFT established a tight, effective control loop. On the other hand, gains on dual-arm tasks were modest (0% $\rightarrow$ 8.3%), indicating that inferring 3D depth and arm-arm collision constraints from monocular RGB images remains a vision-reasoning bottleneck in the base model.

### Zero-Shot Generalization to External Benchmarks and Real Hardware
To verify that the model did not simply memorize simulator environments, it was tested on structurally distinct external benchmarks: LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin 2.0. While the base model achieved zero success, RoboUniverse-35B-A3B accomplished zero-shot completions across all three, demonstrating robust behaviors like autonomously re-grasping dropped objects. Furthermore, deployed zero-shot on a physical Franka arm for a task of drawing an unseen logo on a whiteboard, the model accurately traced the contours while iteratively adjusting the pen-tip height through test strokes.

captions.F9: Overall success rate comparison on RoboUniverse-Verified. SFT on RoboUniverse-10K elevates the base model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) from 0.8% to 21.2%, more than doubling the score of the previous best open-source model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (10.0%).

sections.heading: Comparison with Prior Work: Sim Scale and Agent-Centric Harnesses
sections.summary: In contrast to conventional robot simulators built mostly by hand, this work achieves an unprecedented scale of over 10,000 environments via automated generation from video. It also establishes a fair evaluation protocol for Agentic Robotics that hides ground-truth verifiers and privileged state, providing a post-training infrastructure on par with software engineering.
sections.details:
### The History of Scaling Robot Simulation
Existing simulators such as Meta-World, RLBench, LIBERO, and RoboCasa have supported robot learning for years, but manual scene and reward implementation constrained task counts to dozens or at most a few hundred. Recent efforts have explored generating code via LLMs or 3D reconstruction from real videos (e.g., Real2Gym), but their scale remained small. RoboUniverse-10K pairs automated video-to-sim generation with multi-agent QA to build over 10,000 physically interactive environments for the first time.

### Evaluation Design for Agentic Robotics
Approaches where LLMs write code to control robots (such as Code as Policies) have advanced rapidly, now outperforming VLA models on major benchmarks. However, many conventional evaluation harnesses terminate episodes automatically the moment a success flag is triggered, relieving the agent of judging task completion. Following principles from Embodied First Exam (EFE) and Harbor, this work completely isolates verification code and internal states from the agent, measuring true capabilities by requiring agents to verify task completion visually, just as in the real world.

### Paradigm Shifts in Post-Training and Reinforcement Learning
In software engineering, mining massive executable environments from pull requests to run distillation and reinforcement learning (RLVR), as in Scale-SWE, dramatically enhanced open-source models. While similar efforts are beginning in robotics, the lack of environment scale has been the primary barrier. RoboUniverse-10K resolves this environment deficit, serving as essential infrastructure for large-scale post-training of robot agents.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Work: Long-Horizon Tasks and Dynamic Contact Physics
sections.summary: RoboUniverse-10K establishes the foundation to propel Agentic Robotics into an era of large-scale post-training and rigorous generalization benchmarks. Nonetheless, challenges remain in capturing dynamic contact physics—such as latch friction in appliances from passive video—and in generating long-horizon, multi-stage workflows.
sections.details:
### Conclusion
This work introduces "RoboUniverse-10K," a suite of 10,807 physics environments built via an automated Real2Sim pipeline from real-world videos, alongside "RoboUniverse-Verified," an expert-vetted 500-task zero-shot benchmark. Extensive evaluations uncovered that grasping, cloth manipulation, and post-contact control are primary physical bottlenecks in embodied AI today. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that SFT substantially empowers open-source models, open-sourcing the models and environments to build a solid foundation for future online reinforcement learning.

### Limitations
- **Fidelity of Dynamic Contact Physics**: Currently reconstructed scenes rely heavily on geometric approximations; recovering complex mechanism dynamics—such as the latching resistance of a microwave door or internal hinge friction—purely from passive video remains challenging.
- **Short Task Horizons**: RoboUniverse-10K currently focuses primarily on short, atomic primitive skills. Extending the pipeline to generate long-horizon multi-stage workflows with intricate preconditions and causal dependencies represents a crucial direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix: Harness Specs, Data Breakdown, and Expert Verification
sections.summary: This section summarizes the agent-facing API specifications, task taxonomy breakdowns, and the four-stage manual verification process conducted by 10 experts to ensure benchmark integrity.
sections.details:
### Harness API and Control Interface
The environment is reset only once before the agent starts. The agent is provided with an interface that accepts joint targets rather than end-effector Cartesian poses; inverse kinematics (IK) services are not provided by the environment (the agent must implement or invoke an IK solver within its code). Simulation physics advances only during step execution and pauses while the agent reasons, isolating pure control and reasoning capabilities from inference latency.

### Task Taxonomy and Expert Verification
The 500 tasks in RoboUniverse-Verified were stratified and sampled from candidates passing automated QA, then manually audited by 10 human robotics researchers across four criteria:
- **Instruction Clarity**: Task instructions must be unambiguous and align with the source video.
- **Physical Plausibility**: Mass, friction, collision geometry, and joint limits must be realistic.
- **Replayability**: A reference controller must reliably succeed after resetting the environment.
- **Fairness of Verifiers**: The verifier must reject incorrect behaviors while avoiding false negatives on alternative valid solutions.

Verification logic is strictly structured to return success only when three conditions are met simultaneously: object contact, goal achievement, and remaining stationary after release. This thoroughly prevents cheat solutions or accidental successes.

takeaways: Massive scaling of automatically graded simulation environments that hide privileged state—analogous to SWE-bench—is highly effective for advancing robotic agents.
The fundamental reason open-source models lag behind frontier models is not task comprehension, but the low-level grasping ability to reliably map visual input into joint angles.
Even frontier models struggle significantly with deformable object manipulation (cloth) and millimeter- or Newton-level fine control after contact.

Post-training on high-quality multi-turn trajectories allows models to acquire a structured closed-loop behavior pattern—moving in small increments and visually verifying outcomes—rather than simple memorization.
limitations: Recovering sophisticated contact mechanism dynamics, such as latch resistance or hinge friction, remains difficult purely from passive video estimation.
Current tasks predominantly focus on relatively short atomic manipulation skills, leaving long-horizon multi-step workflows for future work.
Relying solely on monocular RGB images makes the base model's visual reasoning a bottleneck in complex 3D spatial tasks such as dual-arm coordination.
